question: Under Iowa rule 481—2012.1(543B) (formerly 193E—12.1(543B)), which of the following is required of every licensed Iowa sole-proprietor broker, firm, partnership, LLC, association, or corporation, regardless of which types of agency relationships the brokerage chooses to offer?
choice_a: A signed dual agency consent form kept on file for every listing taken, even if dual agency is never used
choice_b: Written pre-approval from the Iowa Real Estate Commission naming which specific agency model the brokerage will use
choice_c: A written company policy identifying and describing the types of real estate brokerage relationships the broker and affiliated licensees may engage in
choice_d: A separate errors-and-omissions insurance rider that specifically covers agency-disclosure claims
explanation: Rule 481—2012.1(543B) requires every licensed brokerage entity to maintain a written company policy identifying and describing the types of brokerage relationships offered, regardless of which relationship types are actually used. The Commission does not pre-approve a brokerage's agency model, dual agency consent forms are only needed when dual agency is actually used, and no special E&O rider is mandated by this rule.

question: Under Iowa's agency disclosure rule, 481—2012.2(543B) (formerly 193E—12.2(543B)), when must a licensee make the required verbal agency disclosure to a client or a nonrepresented customer?
choice_a: Only if the customer specifically asks who the licensee represents
choice_b: Within 24 hours after the first showing of a property
choice_c: At closing, immediately before the closing documents are signed
choice_d: Prior to the licensee providing specific assistance to the client or nonrepresented customer
explanation: Subrule 2012.2(2) requires the verbal disclosure to be made by the licensee prior to providing specific assistance to the client or nonrepresented customer. Disclosure is not conditioned on the customer asking, and it is not deferred to a showing deadline or to closing.

question: An Iowa licensee's initial verbal agency disclosure becomes incomplete, misleading, or inaccurate after her representation status changes mid-transaction. Under subrule 2012.2(3)(b), what is she obligated to do?
choice_a: Immediately give a new verbal disclosure, followed by a new written disclosure signed by all parties to the transaction as soon as practical
choice_b: Nothing, as long as the original written disclosure remains in the file
choice_c: Wait until closing and correct the disclosure within the closing documents
choice_d: Notify only the Iowa Real Estate Commission in writing within 10 days
explanation: Subrule 2012.2(3)(b) requires that a change making the initial written disclosure incomplete, misleading, or inaccurate triggers an immediate new verbal disclosure followed by a new written disclosure signed by all parties as soon as practical. There is no Commission-notification substitute for re-disclosing to the actual parties.

question: Per subrule 2012.2(3)(a) of Iowa's agency disclosure rule, the required written agency disclosure must be made to the buyer or tenant no later than what point?
choice_a: Before the buyer or tenant's first physical walkthrough of the property
choice_b: Before any offer, lease, or rental agreement is made or signed by the buyer or tenant
choice_c: Before the buyer or tenant applies for mortgage pre-approval
choice_d: Before the closing or settlement statement is prepared
explanation: Subrule 2012.2(3)(a) requires the written disclosure to be made to the buyer or tenant before any offer, lease, or rental agreement is made or signed by the buyer or tenant, and before any such document is signed or accepted by the seller or landlord. A walkthrough, a pre-approval application, or the closing statement are not the triggering events under the rule.

question: Under subrule 2012.2(4) and Iowa Code section 543B.57(5), a licensee representing a buyer or tenant on a property that is listed must inform whom of the agency relationship (and whom must the licensee inform if the property is not listed)?
choice_a: Only the buyer's own designated broker, regardless of listing status
choice_b: The Iowa Real Estate Commission, via the annual license renewal form
choice_c: The listing broker or listing agent if the property is listed, or the unrepresented seller or landlord if it is not listed
choice_d: The title company handling the eventual closing
explanation: Subrule 2012.2(4) requires a buyer's or tenant's agent to inform the listing broker, the listing agent, or the seller or landlord (if listed), or the unrepresented seller or landlord (if not listed), consistent with Iowa Code section 543B.57(5). Neither the Commission nor the title company is the required recipient of this disclosure.
source_note: Iowa Admin. Code r. 481—2012.2(543B), subrule 2012.2(4); Iowa Code section 543B.57(5) (formerly 193E—12.2(543B))

question: Under Iowa rule 481—2012.2(543B), subrule 2012.2(5), which statement correctly describes the legal effect of which party pays the broker's compensation?
choice_a: Whichever party pays the commission automatically becomes that broker's client
choice_b: A broker paid by the seller can never simultaneously owe any disclosed duties to the buyer
choice_c: The source of compensation must be separately disclosed to the Iowa Real Estate Commission before every closing
choice_d: The obligation of either the seller/landlord or the buyer/tenant to pay compensation to a broker does not establish or affect any agency relationship
explanation: Subrule 2012.2(5) expressly states that the obligation to pay compensation does not establish or affect any agency relationship. Agency is determined by the disclosed representation, not by the source of the commission.

question: Under subrule 2012.2(6) of Iowa's agency disclosure rule, what does the rule say about written brokerage agreements that add duties beyond the statutory minimums?
choice_a: Nothing in the rule bars a party from entering a written brokerage agreement that contains duties, obligations, and responsibilities in addition to those specified in Iowa license law and commission rules
choice_b: Brokerage agreements may never impose duties beyond the minimums set out in Iowa real estate license law
choice_c: All brokerage agreements exceeding statutory minimums must first be approved by the Real Estate Commission
choice_d: A brokerage agreement automatically terminates if it exceeds the statutory minimum duties
explanation: Subrule 2012.2(6) provides that nothing in the disclosure rule bars parties from contracting for additional duties, obligations, and responsibilities beyond the statutory and rule minimums. There is no Commission pre-approval requirement or automatic-termination consequence.

question: An Iowa licensee represented a client, Maria, as her listing (seller's) agent on one home sale. Months later the same licensee represents Maria again, this time as her buyer's agent purchasing a different property. Under subrule 2012.2(8), is this arrangement permitted?
choice_a: No, a licensee may only ever hold one type of agency relationship with a given client, for the life of that client relationship
choice_b: Yes, a licensee may establish different types of agency relationships with the same client in separate transactions, provided the criteria of Iowa Code chapter 543B and this rule are met for each relationship
choice_c: No, representing the same client in a different capacity automatically creates an undisclosed dual agency violation
choice_d: Only if the Iowa Real Estate Commission pre-approves the second engagement in writing
explanation: Subrule 2012.2(8) expressly permits a licensee to act as seller's agent for a client in one transaction and buyer's agent for that same client in another, so long as the requirements of chapter 543B and the rule are satisfied for each separate transaction. This is not dual agency (which involves representing both sides of the same transaction) and requires no Commission pre-approval.

question: Under subrule 2012.2(9), in which situation is an Iowa licensee NOT required to make an agency relationship disclosure?
choice_a: Whenever the transaction involves a for-sale-by-owner property
choice_b: Whenever the buyer happens to be a licensed real estate agent
choice_c: When the licensee is acting solely as a principal (not as an agent for another) or when a written communication from the licensee is merely a solicitation of business
choice_d: Whenever the transaction's purchase price is under $50,000
explanation: Subrule 2012.2(9) carves out disclosure only where the licensee acts solely as a principal, or where the communication is a business solicitation rather than actual representation. It does not turn on FSBO status, the buyer's own licensure, or price.

question: A seller refuses to sign the agency disclosure document presented by an Iowa licensee. Under subrule 2012.2(10), what must the licensee do?
choice_a: Immediately terminate the listing agreement with the seller
choice_b: Report the refusal to the Iowa Real Estate Commission within 72 hours
choice_c: Proceed as though the disclosure had been signed, since a refusal carries no legal significance
choice_d: Note the refusal, along with the date, place, time, and names of others in attendance, on a copy of the disclosure document, obtain other documentation establishing delivery, and retain the documentation in the transaction file
explanation: Subrule 2012.2(10) requires the licensee to document the refusal in detail on the disclosure document (date, place, time, witnesses) and retain proof of delivery through other means, keeping this documentation in the transaction file. It does not require terminating the listing or reporting to the Commission, and a refusal is not simply disregarded.

question: Under subrule 2012.2(11), for an Iowa licensee offering brokerage services as an auctioneer, what constitutes the "first meaningful contact" with a buyer that triggers the disclosure obligation?
choice_a: The identification of the successful bidder
choice_b: The buyer's registration to bid at the start of the auction
choice_c: The buyer's first phone call inquiring about the auction
choice_d: The recording of the deed after the auction closes
explanation: Subrule 2012.2(11) specifically defines the identification of the successful bidder as the first meaningful contact with a buyer for purposes of triggering disclosure, not mere registration, an inquiry call, or post-closing recording.

question: Per subrule 2012.2(12), how long must an Iowa licensee retain a signed or noted copy of the agency disclosure document in the transaction file, whether the offer was accepted or rejected?
choice_a: 1 year
choice_b: 5 years from the date of the signature or note
choice_c: 2 years
choice_d: 3 years
explanation: Subrule 2012.2(12) sets a five-year retention period from the date of the signature or note, applying whether the offer was ultimately accepted (closed transaction file) or rejected.

question: Under subrules 2012.2(13) and 2012.2(14) of Iowa's agency disclosure rule, what is the stated legal consequence of a licensee's failure to comply with the disclosure rule, or failure to act consistently with disclosure representations already made?
choice_a: It automatically voids the underlying purchase contract
choice_b: It is treated as a strict-liability felony under Iowa Code chapter 543B
choice_c: It constitutes prima facie evidence of a violation of Iowa Code section 543B.34(4)
choice_d: It has no disciplinary consequence unless a civil court first makes an independent finding of fraud
explanation: Subrules 2012.2(13) and 2012.2(14) both state that noncompliance with the disclosure rule, or inconsistency with disclosure representations made, is prima facie evidence of a violation of Iowa Code section 543B.34(4), which is the license-discipline statute — not a basis for automatically voiding the contract or a criminal charge.
source_note: Iowa Admin. Code r. 481—2012.2(543B), subrules 2012.2(13)-(14); Iowa Code section 543B.34(4) (formerly 193E—12.2(543B))

question: Under subrule 2012.2(15), if an Iowa licensee fails to conform to the agency disclosure rule, what effect does the rule say this has on the validity of title to the real property transferred?
choice_a: The transfer becomes automatically voidable by either party for one year
choice_b: The title company must place a lien against the property pending Commission review
choice_c: The buyer may rescind the deed at any time before the licensee's discipline case concludes
choice_d: Nothing in the rule affects the validity of title transferred based solely on the licensee's failure to conform to the disclosure provisions
explanation: Subrule 2012.2(15) explicitly insulates title validity from a licensee's disclosure noncompliance — the rule creates a basis for license discipline against the licensee, not a defect in the conveyance itself.

question: Under subrule 2012.2(17), before entering into a brokerage agreement with a buyer, tenant, seller, or landlord, what must an Iowa licensee disclose to that person in writing?
choice_a: The type or types of brokerage relationships the broker and affiliated licensees are offering to that person
choice_b: The licensee's personal commission split with the designated broker
choice_c: The average days-on-market for comparable listings in the area
choice_d: The licensee's continuing education hours completed that year
explanation: Subrule 2012.2(17) requires written disclosure, before entering a brokerage agreement, of the type(s) of brokerage relationships being offered — this is distinct from, and precedes, the transaction-specific disclosures required later under subrule 2012.2(3).

question: Under Iowa rule 481—2012.5(543B) (formerly 193E—12.5(543B)), a licensee may act as a disclosed dual agent only under what condition, and what happens if a party to the transaction refuses?
choice_a: Only the seller's consent is legally required; the buyer's consent is merely recommended
choice_b: Only with the informed written consent of all parties to the transaction; if any seller, landlord, buyer, or tenant rejects dual agency or refuses to sign consent, the licensee cannot act as a dual agent
choice_c: Consent may be given verbally at closing and need not be reduced to writing
choice_d: Dual agency becomes automatic once a brokerage's company policy permits it, regardless of individual party consent
explanation: Rule 481—2012.5(543B) requires informed written consent from every party before a licensee may act as a disclosed dual agent, and it expressly bars dual agency if any party rejects it or refuses to sign — consent cannot be one-sided, verbal-only, or presumed from company policy alone.

question: Under subrule 2012.5(1)(d), what confidentiality obligation does an Iowa disclosed dual agent owe to each client with respect to the other client's confidential information?
choice_a: The dual agent must share all financial information equally between both clients to remain neutral
choice_b: Confidentiality duties are waived entirely once the dual agency consent agreement is signed
choice_c: The dual agent cannot disclose one client's confidential information to the other client, subject to limited exceptions such as legally mandated disclosure, prevention of fraud/dishonest dealing, or express written authorization
choice_d: The dual agent may disclose either client's confidential information to a competing brokerage if doing so helps close the sale
explanation: Subrule 2012.5(1)(d) preserves each client's confidential information against disclosure to the other client, carving out only narrow exceptions (legal mandate, fraud/dishonesty prevention, or express instruction) — it does not create a duty to share information equally, and signing the consent agreement does not waive confidentiality.

question: Under subrule 2012.5(1)(e), when may an Iowa licensee withdraw from representing a client who has not yet consented to a proposed disclosed dual agency, and what formality applies to that withdrawal?
choice_a: At any time, even after the dual agency relationship has already come into existence
choice_b: Only with prior written permission from the Iowa Real Estate Commission
choice_c: Never; once a listing agreement is signed, withdrawal from a proposed dual agency is prohibited
choice_d: At any time prior to the existence of the dual agency (i.e., before discussing the seller's/landlord's property with the potential buyer/tenant, or vice versa), with the withdrawal made in writing and acknowledged by the clients' separate signatures
explanation: Subrule 2012.5(1)(e) allows withdrawal only before the dual agency relationship actually exists, and requires the withdrawal to be documented in writing with separate client signatures; withdrawal does not require Commission approval and is not barred simply because a listing agreement exists.

question: Iowa Code section 543B.59, implemented by rule 481—2012.6(543B) (formerly 193E—12.6(543B)), authorizes what specific arrangement that distinguishes Iowa's agency framework from a simple disclosed dual agency model?
choice_a: A designated broker's written appointment of one or more different affiliated licensees to act as agent exclusively representing different clients in the same transaction, to the exclusion of all other affiliated licensees in the brokerage
choice_b: A requirement that every in-house transaction must default to disclosed dual agency
choice_c: A blanket prohibition on any brokerage representing both a buyer and a seller in the same transaction under any circumstance
choice_d: A mandate that only the designated broker personally, and never an affiliated licensee, may ever represent either party in an in-house transaction
explanation: Iowa Code section 543B.59 and implementing rule 481—2012.6(543B) create Iowa's "appointed agent" (designated agency) model: the designated broker may appoint different affiliated licensees to represent the seller and buyer separately within the same transaction, each exclusively serving one client. This is distinct from dual agency, where one licensee personally represents both sides.
source_note: Iowa Code section 543B.59; Iowa Admin. Code r. 481—2012.6(543B) (formerly 193E—12.6(543B))

question: Under subrule 2012.7(3), when a designated broker appoints two different affiliated licensees to represent the seller and the buyer respectively in the same transaction (an "appointed agent" arrangement), is the designated broker automatically considered a dual agent?
choice_a: Yes, automatically, because the brokerage as a whole represents both sides of the transaction
choice_b: No, a designated broker is not considered a dual agent solely because the designated broker makes such an appointment, unless the broker personally represents both the seller and buyer (with prior written consent of all parties), in which case dual agency rules apply
choice_c: Yes, but only if the transaction involves residential property
choice_d: No, but only if the Iowa Real Estate Commission grants a waiver in advance
explanation: Subrule 2012.7(3) clarifies that merely appointing separate affiliated licensees to represent opposing clients does not make the designated broker a dual agent; dual agent status and its associated duties attach only if the broker personally, with prior written consent, represents both sides. No Commission waiver is needed for the appointed-agent structure itself, and the rule is not limited to residential transactions.
